utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. And good afternoon, Professor. The affirmation you made at the commencement of your evidence still applies. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor Taseva.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I proceed with my questions, let me inform you that in accordance with your suggestions, I believe that I will complete my examination before the first break. In order for me not to interrupt my examination, I would like the witness and Their Honours to be given the remainder of the documents that the Defence has prepared and which are related only to the documents matching the footnotes of the expert witness and can be of service for easier bearings in the expert report of Professor Taseva. I should like Madam Professor to have her first binder before her where her report is to be found at the beginning of the binder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, at page 18 of the report, paragraphs 64 and 65, you stated your opinion as to the concept of operative control and operational control. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the concept operational control, you state that this was the first time you heard of that notion. Is that the position you presented in the mentioned paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I listed in the report is in fact that I have never heard of this concept of control, that it can be applied in the work of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If someone were to state the opposite before this Tribunal, would that individual be in fact familiar with the structure and the modus operandi of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This concept of this type of control is mostly linked with the work of the army. This is why I believe that if someone were to claim that this type of control or this concept of control exists in the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Macedonia, then that someone would not have sufficient knowledge about the positioning of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Taseva, does the term of operative control exist at all in the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the police, there is the notion of operative control.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 65 ter 1D1232, which is page 1D9888. In the English version, 1D9893.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, do you know what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an obligatory instruction from the Ministry of Interior which is in force there as of 1976.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, does this document stipulate the notion of operative control in the police sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The aim of this document is exactly this, to establish the notion and the manner in which this type of operative work in the Ministry of Interior is applied. It contains and it defines the concept of operative control.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the following page, 1D9889, and 1D9894.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 31 of the document, precisely what you stated is being established, the notion of operative control in the police sense. And item 31 says: "Operative control is a sum of operative-preventative measures that are being taken based on general information or knowledge and with the aim of preventing the perpetration of criminal acts the surveillance of certain persons with a propensity to commit criminal acts and observation of specific facilities and points where criminal offences are committed." Is this definition consistent with your knowledge of operative control in the police sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This definition is consistent with my knowledge of the operative control in the police sense of the word, or in the sense of police work, and in this context it is applied in the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In item 32 it is stated that operative control is established with regard to an individual, facility or a point. Is that also the basis of your conclusion from paragraph 65 and footnote 52 -- or, rather, that you stated as a source in that footnote?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the basis for my conclusion and the listing in the footnote.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, if I were to say that oftentimes a single term can have several different meanings and that it is of essential importance to clarify the basic meaning of a word, would you, as an academician agree with me, or, rather, let me put the question to you: Is it important to know the actual meaning and significance or sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we wish to be precise in what we do, both as scholars but also as professionals, then we have to have to deal with clearly defined notions and terms about occurrences which we wish to observe. This is why I believe that definitions are very important when we want to research or delineate certain notions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to show the witness 65 ter 1D12761, page 1D0215 -- apologies. 65 ter 1D1276. And the page is 1D0215. This is an excerpt from a dictionary that the translation service of this Tribunal sent to the Defence with regard to the possible meaning of the word "control." This is a dictionary that the translation service makes use of in translating significant documents and all the text that transpire or appear before this Tribunal. Madam Professor, in the entry for the word "kontrola," or control, which is in the top part of the page, there's the word "control." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Next, various meanings of the word are listed. In other words, the possible translations of the Macedonian word "kontrola." Please cast an eye on this page, and I want you to focus only on the word "kontrola." And tell me, which of the translations match the meaning of "kontrola" in the context in which it is used in the police of the Republic of Macedonia? And, of course, that's the term we used that earlier on when we looked at the document entitled obligatory instruction, which deals with control.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the screen and in the context of the definition of operative control in the obligatory instruction, I believe that operative control used in the work of the police in the Republic of Macedonia is best defined by point 2, proverka, check, inspection, supervision of check-points. What is listed under the point 2. To carry out inspection, what is listed again in item 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Professor Taseva, I would like to move to a different topic. At pages 20 to 26 and in paragraphs 76 through 99 in chapters 7 and 8, you stated your opinions and conclusions with regard to the role of the Ministry of Interior and the minister in the procedure which proceeds the criminal proceedings and in the investigating procedure. In these paragraphs, if I may summarize in one sentence, you spoke of the role of the Ministry of Interior in the pre-crime procedure, in the investigation and criminal reporting. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall us examining and discussing in -- yesterday Article 170 of the criminal procedure act, P78 [as interpreted], which lists the obligation of the judiciary bodies to file a criminal report with regard to offences. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that we spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In -- that's in line 26, instead of P78, it should state P88. Could the witness be shown P88, but this time, Article 142. 0019057 is the page; and in the English version, ERN 0019209, or page 33 out of 128.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the Article before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the way this legal provision is formulated we will see that it says: If there is ground for suspicion that the crime is committed which is to be prosecuted ex officio, and next the actions to be taken by the Ministry of Interior are listed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown Exhibit P96. That's the rule governing the performance of duties in the Ministry of Interior, in particular Article 103 of the rules, which is to be found at page ERN 0424638. Unfortunately, I don't have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have both the Macedonian and English versions on the screen now. The initial information about the perpetrated criminal offence is discussed here and in Article 103 it is stated again: When there exists grounds for suspecting that a crime, has been committed which is prosecuted ex officio, the authorised officials shall take necessary measures and so on and so forth. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with what we were able to see yesterday and what we've just read, I want to ask you the following: Does such a definition of the competences and responsibilities of the Ministry of the Interior have anything to do with the criminal offences prosecuted ex officio and for reasonable suspicion of a crime having been committed?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All provisions which we read yesterday and today pertain to criminal acts which are prosecuted ex officio and for the reasonable grounds, reasonable suspicions of a crime having been committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Professor, can you tell me which are the criminal offences prosecuted ex officio, speaking in general?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, criminal acts which are prosecuted ex officio are part or are under the category of serious crimes, which provide for jail sentences over one year, and for which there are classified forms of criminal acts in the criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, are there some other criminal offences which are not prosecuted ex officio?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the criminal code of the Republic of Macedonia, there are such criminal acts which the -- the prosecution of which can be undertaken by way of a private suit or at the proposal of the injured party who submits a proposal that the competent bodies prosecute this person, which means that there two additional means by which this procedure can be initiated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of one such criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most frequently, and statistically speaking, where the private suit is undertaken is slight bodily harm, where the law defines clearly which serious bodily crime is defined. But in the case of slight bodily harm, then prosecution is undertaken by a legal suit initiated by the injured party.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. I'm aware of the section on ex officio crimes begins at paragraph 79 and goes through paragraphs 85, Your Honour, but I must say that this information that the witness has just given that certain -- certain criminal acts they should or may be taken over by way of private suit by the injured party, it's my understanding is nowhere within the text of this expert report and it is certainly a significantly new issue that's now being raised here that I haven't seen raised before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor Taseva, now that you've explained the first requirement, when we were reading the provisions you quoted in the footnotes as the basis for your conclusions and opinions, is the second requirement such that the police should act upon reasonable grounds for suspicion that a given act does in fact constitute a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm following the translation, so I don't know whether this corresponds to what we are discussing, but I believe that you were asking --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking whether it is necessary for the second requirement to be met, the one we -- which we read in Articles 140, 142 and 143, whereby there are reasonable grounds for suspicion. Is that a precondition for the Ministry of the Interior to act upon its duties and competencies?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If the competencies of the Ministry of the Interior could be defined, if we are saying that there is reasonable ground for suspicion that a criminal offence has been committed, one that is prosecuted ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can Professor now look at Article 104 of the same rules. I will read out to you what is written here before I put my question to you. Article 104: "In order to confirm the existence of grounds for suspicion that a crime has been committed, it is necessary that specific relevant facts and data be known on the basis of which it can reasonably be assumed that a crime has been committed. "The assumptions pointing to the fact that an event is a result of a crime must be based on specific facts that show that this event has taken place and that it contains elements of criminal activity." Tell me, Professor Taseva, is this definition of the reasonable grounds for suspicion consistent with the opinion you advanced in your report, and is it consistent with your experience and knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The definition that you read out now fully corresponds to what my report has advanced, but it is also the basis for the practice in the operation of the Ministry of the Interior. So, in the practice, my experience from my work in the Ministry of Interior shows and confirms that it is preceded pursuant to this provision that we are reading and this rule book.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, at which point is the Ministry of the Interior obligated to report a given act to the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior needs to inform the public prosecutor in charge once it receives certain information on a given event, but after it undertakes preliminary measures to ascertain, firstly, whether this event has really taken place, what kind of event that was, whether that event constitutes a crime. So whether it does contain elements of an accident, incident, or is it -- does it contain elements of criminal activity. After the Ministry of Interior finds certain elements or indications that a crime has been committed that corresponds to the provisions of the law, corresponds to the incriminations prosecuted by law, then it will inform the public prosecutor, regardless of whether it is a crime perpetrated by a known perpetrator or by an unknown perpetrator. Also, the Ministry of the Interior will inform the public prosecutor in all cases when there are crimes to suspect when there are so indications or evidence that a death has occurred. It might be a natural death, if a person is found dead, regardless of whether or of what was the cause of death, the ministry has a duty to inform the public prosecutor immediately and the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From that point, Professor Taseva, when the ministry notifies the investigating judge or prosecutor thereof, what -- in what way does the ministry proceed from there? Independently or upon someone's order?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Macedonia, after the public prosecutor receives the information, it could be a special information note or a criminal report, from that moment onwards the competent justice system bodies are in charge of the procedure. That would mean the public prosecutor and the investigating judge, but in our system the public prosecutor is the dominus litis in the criminal procedure. He is in charge of the entire procedure from then onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Professor, since we're still discussing the preliminary procedure in which the prosecutor is the one controlling the normal course of proceedings, if in that particular procedure the information that reaches the ministry you mentioned the occurrence of a death or let us take another example, that the police were informed that in the elementary school in Kocani drugs were being sold or that there has been illicit trafficking in weapons, if, upon receiving such information, the police has been unable to obtain any relevant evidence confirming the authenticity of the event or information, does the police still have the standing obligation to notify the public prosecutor thereof?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the cases when the Ministry of the Interior has information available or when it receives information that something is taking place, such as in the examples that you indicated, in that case it will undertake measures and activities from within the range of their competencies to receive more substantiated information, to gather evidence or indications that would lead to reasonable grounds to believe that a crime has been committed. Just for the sake of illustration or to follow up on what we discussed previously, usually in the cases, like in the examples that gave, the ministry will institute operational control in order to gather full spectrum of information in a given event.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please answer this question: If the ministry does not obtain any information, does it still have the obligation to inform the public prosecutor? If, therefore, the efforts invested into the verifying of the information prove fruitless, is the ministry still duty-bound to inform the public prosecutor thereof?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry can sometimes spend a long period of time in gathering information or in attempt to -- attempts to gather information, but still be fruitless and in such cases it is does not have the obligation to inform the public prosecutor. Until the moment that it has specific information that would be reasonable ground to suspect a crime has been committed, it has no obligation to inform public prosecutor of such developments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the event the public prosecutor, who may have also obtained the sort of information I mentioned, seeks the Ministry of Interior to make inquiries into that particular information, in that event, does the Ministry of Interior have the obligation to inform the prosecutor of the information that it has in its possession?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since the request -- or, actually the public prosecutor could also arrive at certain information and then ask for further information from the Ministry of the Interior and request that certain actions be taken as well. In such cases, the ministry has the duty to inform the public prosecutor about everything that it has or the information it lacks on a specific case. So even in such cases when it has no information that would corroborate that suspicion that a crime has been committed, the ministry has the duty to submit the information to the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If, Professor Taseva, the prosecutor or the judge have all the relevant information pointing to the fact that these reports were truthful, either through the information they received from the police or through an on-site investigation or through the judge or the prosecutor going to visit and interview the person concerned or injured in the hospital, would the police have the obligation to send once more the criminal report to the same bodies, based on the information that they have thus gathered?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such cases the Ministry of Interior has no obligation to file a criminal report with the competent justice system bodies. It could only proceed by submitting information that it itself is able to arrive at. A citizen could come to the police, come to the ministry, to give out information related to an event, and in such case the ministry can communicate that information to the justice system bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If, in such ensuing situation the prosecutor and judge asked the ministry to act on their own initiative in that regard, would the ministry be duty-bound to do so?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In a situation when the justice system bodies have the case, are in charge of the case, whenever they would request that the Ministry of the Interior undertake some action, it has the duty to do so, and with regards to the activities undertaken and the results thereof, inform the public prosecutor or the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in connection with this witness's answer, I refer you to 1D67, 1D68, 1D69, 1D70, P54.052, P54.027, P54.028, P54.029, and P54.030.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, Professor Taseva, and let me ask you this one question. In your CV, you stated that you authored the book, Dark Number of Criminality. In the book you state that you carried out some investigation in that regard.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That book was written in 1995 and for it I researched several types of criminality and the dark figures related to certain types of crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, your findings in that book testify to what precisely? What is the figure of undetected crime?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The results of those researches point that in regards to all times of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this line of questioning to the issues in this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the course of this trial, on several occasions it was discussed that efforts were being invested into detecting crime and it has been stated that measures were not taken to punish the crime committed and that's why I wanted to ask the expert witness about this since this was the topic that she dealt with in the book that she listed in her CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter adds that Madam Residovic said that it was one of the counts of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, apparently this was a book written by the witness in 1995, so I'm not sure how her research in 1995 would be applicable to the relevant time-period in 2001 and 2002. And it's simply seems to the Prosecution that the issues in this case, vis-a-vis the indictment point to, for example, the third element of criminal responsibility, the material ability to investigate the crime and punish the perpetrators. But the Prosecution still does not see about a general book from 1995 related to research on crime statistics is going to help advance the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Your Honour, may I address you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One last time, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, the professor speaks in that book about the role of the accused in the -- of the injured person in the detection of the crimes committed and that's the topic I should like to examine the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We uphold the objection of Mr. Saxon, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the witness be shown Exhibit 1D189.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Professor, you have before you an Official Note written by the department of the Ministry of Interior in Cair, which contains a piece of information which states the following: "On the 15th of November 2001, according to the OVR Cair, an interview was made with Selim Ljuboten about the events that took place on the 12th of August, 2001, in the village of Ljuboten during which in the fights between the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia and the terrorist gangs stationed in the village, eight individuals died." Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The information that in some clashes eight individuals were killed, in correlation with your testimony of a moment ago, would that be sufficient to establish the suspicion that the death has been a result of a crime?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see here deals with an event that took place on the stated date, but from what is written in this specific Official Note, one could still not say whether a crime has been committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, what else would be needed to ascertain the grounds for suspicion that the death of those individuals is a result of a crime perpetrated?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, it has to be ascertained, first, what was the nature of that event, what actually took place, because here also it is written "event." The word itself, "event" is not sufficient to learn about the nature of the event and to further establish whether there are some elements that would indicate that there has been some criminal conduct or that a crime has been committed. In this case, several measures need be to undertaken to ascertain what was the nature of the event, who participated in the event, what took place and how, or why did it happen, so all those questions need to be answered for us to see what was the nature of that event. As it is, we can't know whether it was a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if it is not possible to immediately inspect the crime scene and see the dead bodies, what would be necessary to establish the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there are dead bodies, the best measure would be to carry out autopsy immediately after the event. But if it has not been done, if the persons have been buried on the same date, as it is written here, then it would be necessary to request exhumation to then ascertain the cause of death and the way in which the death occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Without those elements that you described now, would the police be able to verify whether the event has really taken place and what was the nature of that event, whether it contains elements of criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously this is an event that goes beyond the scope of work of the Ministry of the Interior and beyond the scope of work of the police, because it is indicated here that this has been an event where the individuals -- where the results in such case the -- immediately the justice system bodies are informed, the public prosecutor and the investigating judge, and they could -- and they actually have the obligation under the law to undertake all necessary measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the Exhibit P104.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We have here yet another Official Note, Professor Taseva, and it deals with an interview with Kenan Salievski. We can see here that on the 15th of November, 2001, in the OVR Cair, Kenan Salievski was interviewed first regarding the events and information related to those, and that person said that he had information and that would convey those information. And the final paragraph says: "This is why it was agreed that the person would come on the 16th of November, on the next day, and bring complete lists. On the 16th of November, 2001, Kenan Salievski called us at the department for internal affairs, Cair, and told us that after having consulted the village board from the village Ljuboten, he cannot give us any information about the event or about the deceased persons." Madam Professor, considering what you stated before, if the injured parties or individuals who have any information regarding the event are unwilling to communicate those information to the Ministry of the Interior or to the police, would that fact and to what extent would that fact make the clarification of an event more difficult and would it make more difficult to ascertain whether it constitutes a crime or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often the police or the Ministry of Interior, information about criminal acts receives from injured persons in such cases, we have the initial grounds to act or the police has the initial grounds to act because the injured parties are interested in further proceeding in order to uncover the perpetrator of this criminal act. If this Official Note which we see here is the usual way of acting on the part of the MOI, and in accordance with the obligatory instruction to collect as much information as possible about the event at hand, to interview persons who know something about this event or have data regarding this event, but here it is obvious that the person with whom contact was established, after consultation with other persons, decided that he should not provide any kind of information about the event or about the deceased persons. In such cases, indeed, it is more difficult to work and establish all elements regarding this event and in order to establish whether we have a criminal act at hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Professor Taseva, I would move now to the final topic that I wish to discuss with you. On page 30, in paragraphs 125 to 128, you spoke about the Law on Amnesty. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if I understood what is written here correctly, and I believe you made it very clear, the law does not make any difference especially it does not introduce any discrimination with regards to the ethnicity of the persons subject to amnesty. Basically, the amnesty applies to all individuals who committed crimes related to the conflict and the only exception are the crimes that are within the competence of this Tribunal. Would that be the brief summary of what you stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this, tell me, Professor Taseva, during that time was a state of war declared during that time, in the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time in the Republic of Macedonia a state of war was not proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, pursuant to the legislation of the Republic of Macedonia, the state of war or state of a military conflict, would that constitute the basis or necessary prerequisite for the application of martial law?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now show you part of the statement of a witness who testified before this court, Vilma Ruskovska, page 1528. And on the question whether state of war was declared in Macedonia, in line 12, she said: "It was not declared."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you, Ms. Residovic. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but again I must object. There is nothing within the remit of this report, or, I believe, within the questions asked of the witness related to the constitutionality and constitutional procedures of -- related to declaring states of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the amnesty was introduced because of the crimes related to the conflict. My next questions will be related to this but probably I need to ask some introductory questions, although it was not specifically stated in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I say, Mr. Saxon, you will have discerned that we are following the course generally of allowing questions that may have relevance to the issues in the case, even though they may not be subject to specific reference in the report of the witness. And we're doing so on the basis, which I was to indicate to you at the end of the evidence, that if you find you are not prepared to cross-examine on one of those issues, then some time may be necessary to allow to you make that preparation. What has happened so far would not suggest any particular length of time was needed, but that opportunity will be there and it may be that some issue will arise that will involve the need for a longer time in preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please carry on, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just stress, because I did say so, and I thank the Chamber for the opportunity to ask those questions. With regards to the state of war and whether it has been declared, the professor did say something in paragraph 16; but I do agree that she did not speak of that exclusively. So, Professor Taseva, I will continue reading what I started reading. That is the statement of Vilma Ruskovska that she gave on the 6th of June before this Tribunal. And since she confirmed that the state of war was not declared, she was asked the following question: "[In English] Because these were isolated terrorist attacks and because no state of war had been declared in the country, the criminal proceeding you participate in were carried out according to the domestic law." [Interpretation] And she then said: "[In English] Yes." [Interpretation] And then the question again: "[In English] At that time you, as a deputy prosecutor, your colleague and judge in the court before which you were acting were not even considering applying international humanitarian law to certain evidence. Would that be correct?" [Interpretation] And the answer was yes. Professor Taseva, was that witness statement given before this Tribunal consistent to your knowledge of the way in which the then state bodies and justice system bodies treated the situation of the country and the application of the domestic law?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They're quite consistent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, for an act to be qualified as a war crime against civilian population, pursuant to the law of the Republic of Macedonia, would it be necessary for that -- that the state of war or the state of a military conflict is declared?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will kindly ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit P81, Article 404. That is war crime against civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this Article? The Macedonian page is N000-26 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the counsel to read the number slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I will draw your attention, Professor Taseva, to the first line in this Article which says: "A person, who, by violating the rules of international law, during a war, armed conflict or occupation," and then various acts are enumerated that could constitute war crime against civilian population. Does it correspond to your knowledge of the situations when these provisions are applied?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the middle of this Article, you can see various types or ways in which crimes could be committed. And in line 7 from the top in the Macedonian text are mentioned murders, torture, inhumane treatment. Then, towards the bottom there is theft of property, wilful destruction of various properties. Tell me, Professor Taseva, would these offences exist also as independent crimes in the Criminal Code of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These criminal acts do exist in other provisions of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just for the transcript, I will mention that in P81, murder is article 123, grievous bodily harm is Article 131, ordinary bodily injury is Article 130, that is prosecuted against a private complaint. Then, theft and aggravated theft are 135 and -- 235 and 236. Bodily injury qualified by death is Article 131, paragraph 3, torture is Article 142, crime against general population is Article 288. No, we will not show anything because we have sufficient time to close this part.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regards to what we discussed now, if some individuals were perpetrators of these crimes that I have enumerated now, murder, aggravated robbery, torture, et cetera, would those crimes be amnestied, pursuant to the Law on Amnesty?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in accordance with the Law on Amnesty these persons would be amnestied.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What would be the only thing that would not be subject to amnesty?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crimes against civilian population that would be done in normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the law of the Republic of Macedonia, who makes the legal assessment what would an event mean? Who would make the legal assessment whether something is to be called a crime, crime of theft, or burglary, for instance, or would it be a murder or a war crime? What is the body that gives the legal interpretation, assessment? What is the criminal offence at hand?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The final instance which gives the legal interpretation about the act at hand are the courts and the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are the courts bound by the legal characterisation that the prosecutor has provided?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public prosecutor can provide a legal qualification when it submits the charges to the courts but the courts are not tied to that statement of the Prosecutor when they make their own assessment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the counsel and the witness to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, with regards to amnesty, you spoke about that in paragraphs 125 and 128, you stated here that this was an important aspect of the Ohrid Framework Agreement and the aim was to restore peace, to avoid retaliations and to achieve social reintegration. Is that your opinion as stated in the aforementioned paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my opinion presented in those paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, several exhibits were led before this court which indicate that a criminal procedure does not preclude simultaneous disciplinary procedure and I will not ask you in relation to this. But having in mind the objectives that the amnesty was to achieve, tell me, please, if I give you a hypothetical case, for instance, an Albanian police officer joined the NLA, took a gun and fought against his country. The Law on Amnesty has amnestied that crime and he returned to his post in his police station. However, if we're looking at the collective agreement and you quoted from this several times, he violated the working discipline. He was absent from work and so a disciplinary procedure should run against him and he should be dismissed from his post. Tell me, please, in such hypothetical situation, would the goals of the amnesty that you spoke in your report about be achieved?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A case such as this would defeat the purpose of the Law on Amnesty and would not further the objectives of this law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And such cases could apply to Macedonians, Albanians, Turks and any one else who would be amnestied for a crime but then sanctioned in a disciplinary procedure. Is this consistent with your position?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Law on Amnesty does not make a difference on any basis, not even an ethnic one. And it -- measures like this should not be implemented further or the distinctions be made.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask again the witness and counsel to avoid overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well done, Ms. Residovic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be convenient, would it, Mr. Saxon, to have the first break at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will do that and resume, then, at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender two documents into evidence, namely, 65 ter 1D1232, of which the professor spoke in paragraph 65, footnote 52, which is the obligatory instruction. And the other one is 65 ter 1D1276, which is an excerpt from a dictionary that the Defence received from the CLSS and in relation to which the professor explained the meaning of control in the police context. I informed the Prosecutor about this over the break and now I understood that they don't have an objection to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Each of those documents will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D1232 will become Exhibit 1D311; 65 ter 1D1276 will become Exhibit 1D312, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if the Chamber wants to inquire whether my colleague Mr. Apostolski has any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not an indication but it should be on the record. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I believe that the Court has made good assessment in that I will not be having any questions for this witness. Therefore, I give my time over to my learned colleague, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Apostolski, for the second or could be the third time of asking, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Taseva. My name is Dan Saxon and I represent the Prosecutor in these proceedings. Originally, I'm from the city of Boston in the United States. And there are a few topics that I like to discuss with you, if I may. First of all, I have a few questions that relate to your -- your background and experience as they're outlined in your CV, which I note is now Exhibit 1D109. From 1981 to 2000, you worked in the Ministry of the Interior of Macedonia as an analyst. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And now that I know that we're going to be speaking in the same language, I need to give you the same caution that my colleague gave you, that you and I need to pause briefly between our questions and answers so that we do not create difficulties for the interpreters, all right. During that period 1981 to 2000 when you were employed by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, did you ever arrest anyone?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During that period, did you ever personally carry out an investigation into a crime?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I personally did not head an investigation of a crime -- of a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, even if you didn't head an investigation, did you participate in one?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you ever take part in any combat-related activities?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never taken part in any combat-related activities, except in exercises of this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And if I can just step back for moment, when you participated in the investigation of a crime, what exactly was your role? What things did you do? Can you give some examples?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the cases of more serious crimes, such as murder, it was usual that an analyst go to the site where an on-site investigation is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so is that the kind of -- if I can use the term, would that be called operative work or an operative activity?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operative works were taken by other colleagues who were charged with such tasks. My task and the task of other colleagues, analysts, when taking part in activities and procedures such as these, was to pay attention to everything that was being done so that when everything was being completed and if it was necessary to file a case towards the necessary -- the competent judicial bodies to make sure that everything was included and nothing was omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say, then, that although you were not precisely performing operative works, it was part of your job to observe operative works?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the years when you were working for the Ministry of Internal Affairs, did you ever -- were you ever a participant in the collegium of the minister?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never been a member of the minister's collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 2001 and 2002, did you perform any activities with members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time I was not employed at the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the course of your anti-corruption activities -- let me step back. It's very clear from your CV that you have also played a leading role in the fight against corruption in Macedonia since 2000/2001. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the course of your anti-corruption work, did you ever provide any assistance to government ministries or an entity or agency of the government of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify the question? What kind of assistance or cooperation are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, for example, did you ever provide any advice to a particular ministry or government body as to how they might more effectively combat corruption within their ministry.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in the preparation of the state programme for prevention of corruption, which contains a number of measures and activities which pertain to a large number of state institutions, but also to other factors in the fight against corruption. Therefore, in the course of my work, I have had communication and contacts with all ministries, part of the state administration, with the judicial bodies, with the media, and with all others that have a role in the fight against corruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during -- and in that -- just so that the record is clear, at that time you were -- you were the director, for example, of a non-governmental organisation?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2001, I was the executive director of the branch of Transparency International in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When did you begin to have these communications and contacts with different ministries and state administration and with judicial bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period, from November 2002 to February 2007, I was a member of the state commission for prevention of corruption. In this capacity, I had contacts with all state bodies. However, I would also like to add that the goal of the non-governmental sector is also to assist the government in defining its measures and activities in a given domain. Thus, is to be understood the work of participation of the civil sector in the state administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely, I understand that. Can you give a couple of examples of the kinds of contacts and communications you had then with some state bodies about issues of corruption, if you gave any advice, gave any assistance, whatever?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I could not point out anything in particular because such contacts were plentiful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And in the course of those contacts, at times, for example, you provided some advice, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible and it is probable. I have taken part in many activities as a member of working bodies, working groups where I gave my opinions, where I have given advice most probably, based on my viewpoints and assessments, so this is not to be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you were giving your advice in some situations, you were not an employee of the government institution who you were giving advice to, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it would be better if you could be a little bit more specific. I cannot respond to such abstract questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that was an abstract question at all. I think it was a very simple question. When you gave advice to members of government institutions during your anti-corruption activities, you were not an employee of the institution who you were advising, were you? It's not an abstract question. It only requires a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that I was not employed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Since 2004, you have been the director of the police academy in Macedonia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And am I correct that the police academy is an entity that is part of the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not correct. The police academy is a part of the university and it is not part of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And over the past years, several years, since you have been director of the police academy, the police academy has received financial assistance and technical assistance from different international institutions, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we're very proud of this fact. Because this was the only way for the institution which had previously been closed for ten years to be revived and to be able to be an institution that maintains all standards necessary for this type of work and this type of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, for example, for several years there was a group part of the European Union called the EU Proxima mission which sent police advisors to Macedonia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a number of years in Macedonia, the mission of Proxima was active.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did members of EU Proxima, for example, provide some assistance in the police academy?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I'm not specifically sure that from the time that I was there they had activities in the police academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you aware that in recent years members of the EU Proxima police mission had been providing technical assistance to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they worked together with the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in fact they worked very closely with members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Of course, these members of this European Union mission that are assigned to provide assistance to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, they're not employees of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, are they?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were employed -- or, rather, engaged by the European Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Moving to a different topic, professor. Yesterday - it's at page 53 of the LiveNote transcript. I'm sorry, I don't have the final transcript reference. In response to a question from my colleague Ms. Residovic, you said that when attempting to surpress criminal behaviour committed by organised groups or when attempting to solve complex crimes, there may be close coordination between several bodies of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And, Professor, you also explained that these matters may be addressed by using "a direct link with the structures at the Ministry of Interior by chain of command towards the centre in the Ministry of Interior." And I just -- if you could, please, help us understand. Can you explain what you mean by the phrase "the chain of command towards the centre in the Ministry of Internal Affairs."

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having said "chain of command," because there's no such thing in the ministry. This is a chain of coordination. If you allow me to elaborate on the structure of the Ministry of Interior, perhaps this would become more clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, we've heard a lot of evidence about the structure of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. But just so that your testimony is clear, are you saying that the concept of a chain of command, that concept does not exist or in 2001 did not exist within the Ministry of Internal Affairs? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is so. This concept does not exist now, did not exist when I was working there, nor in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is 65 ter Exhibit 956.8.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we have prepared some binders this afternoon for your reading pleasure. And if we could perhaps distribute what is the fourth binder that we have to the Chamber, my colleagues, and one for the witness. And this particular document will be found at tab 286 in this fourth binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Maybe before I ask you a question about this document, Professor Taseva, this concept of chain of command, although I understand you say it does not exist within the Ministry of Internal Affairs, but you have heard -- you've heard the term before, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have heard the term, but it is not used in the work of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree with me that on a very simple level, conceptually, when people talk about a chain of command, they refer to subordinates reporting up a chain, and then superiors issuing orders going down the chain.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the chain of command means issuing direct orders and receiving feedback information on these direct orders for undertaking specific measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Isn't that what I just said basically, Professor Taseva? Someone reports information up to their superior and then their superior, acting on that information, issues a direct order down the chain. Isn't that what I just said?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are explaining the concept of command, which is not the concept of coordination and cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the concept of coordination and cooperation. I'm trying to explore with you what you said a few minutes ago, that the concept of chain of command does not exist in the Ministry of Interior, all right? Are we clear on that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now, would you agree with me that in simplistic terms, and forget about the Ministry of Internal Affairs for the purposes of my question, all right, in simplistic terms when someone refers to a chain of command, they refer to a subordinate sending information up the chain and a superior acting on that information, and sending orders down a chain. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, if you ask me personally, the term "chain of command" immediately associates a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Fine. I'll use your understanding, okay? Let's speak in a -- if you want, let's think about the army right now, the army of the Republic of Macedonia, all right? Now when you think about the term "chain of command," could involve people, yes, wearing uniforms, all right, we think about subordinates reporting information up the chain to their superiors; and we think about superiors acting on that information and issuing orders down the chain, to their subordinates. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Issuing orders in a military sense of the word is something which does not go together with the word "information."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness and counsel to pause between question and answer, otherwise the witness's answers do not get into Macedonian broadcast channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, you and I have been politely asked to pause between our questions and answers, all right. It probably won't be the first time that we'll be politely asked. Can you please explain your last answer. Why doesn't issuing orders go together with the word "information"? Why don't those two concepts go together?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because issuing orders for undertaking specific measures, according to my understanding, and I'm not a military expert, goes hand in hand with writing reports about the activities related to those specific orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if someone at higher up in a chain of command receives a report - again I'll use your term - someone higher up in a chain of command is sent a report by subordinates lower down in the chain of command. And then the person at the high end of the chain of command acts upon that report and issues an order down the chain of command. That's usually what we think happens when we think about a chain of command, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while back we were speaking about the terms and the necessity to explain how they're used. Perhaps the same should be done in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I think what I'd like you to do, please, is take a look either on your screen or at the document in tab 286. This document is an information dated the 10th of June, 2001, to the analytics and investigations sector of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on reports received by the headquarters of operation Ramno, operative action Ramno, in connection with the current situation in the Republic of Macedonia, between 0700 hours and 1500 hours on 10 June, 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. However, if you allow me, I will point out to the problems in translation. In the Macedonian language, the word "istrazuvanje" in this case should be translated as "research," and not "investigation." Because this is the sector for analytics and research.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Can you see, in the middle of the page, we see a paragraph beginning: "On 10 June " -- actually, it would be the fourth paragraph from the top, beginning with SVR Kumanovo. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "SVR Kumanovo informed by telephone that on 10 June 2001 at approximately 1240 hours, three army of the Republic of Macedonia soldiers ... were wounded." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then it says: "Another three soldiers were wounded at 1345 hours in the region of Gosince." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And can we turn to the last page, please. In both languages, hopefully. Thank you. And then we see that this research, I'll use your term, has been dispatched to the minister of the interior, the deputy minister, the state secretary, the director of security and counter-intelligence division, the director of the public safety bureau, chief of the police department, chief of the criminal police department, and the headquarters of operative action Ramno. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is Exhibit P468. And, Your Honour, at this time because this document is contained in the second binder, we will -- I retract what I just said, Your Honour. I'm just going to depend on e-court for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see, Professor, this is a telegram from the cabinet of the minister of the Ministry of Interior. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it's dated the 11th of June, the day after the document I showed you just a minute ago, and it's directed to the sector of finances in Kocani and the sector for analytics and investigation. And it's signed by then minister Ljube Boskoski. You see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. It is addressed to the SVR, Kocani, to the Sector for Finance and Other Joint Administrative Services of the MOI. That would mean to the minister and to the sector for analytics and research within the MOI.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And it says that in order to undertake security measures in the territory of Macedonia in replacement of police forces, it is needed that on the 12th of June, 2001, 50 policemen and Mitko Sapolovski, their senior officer in charge, be transferred to the military barracks in Kumanovo. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then it gives a description of how the policemen should be equipped, what they should take with them, et cetera. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, can you agree with me that this instruction is -- or this telegram has been issued in response to the news from Kumanovo that was sent to the minister on the day before?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have no basis to agree with you. It would take -- I couldn't agree with your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if the minister of the interior receives information on the 10th of June that a number of persons have been injured in fighting on that day around Kumanovo, and then on the 11th of June issues this telegram to get 50 policemen, 50 more policemen in combat gear sent up to Kumanovo, doesn't common sense tell you that there might be a connection between the two documents?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have insufficient elements to establish the link between the two documents, and from what is written in the first sentence of this document, I see that it relates to the entire territory of Macedonia, not one specific sector for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if you could read it a little bit more carefully, Professor, in that first paragraph you will see that the minister is instructing that 50 policemen and their senior officer be transferred to the military barracks in Kumanovo, not to anywhere in the Republic of Macedonia. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see is that the purpose or the preamble, if you will, reads: In order to undertake security measures in the territory of the Republic of Macedonia. And the notion that they were sent to the Kumanovo barracks does not mean that the security measures that need to be undertaken would be undertaken in Kumanovo. That could be just the place where from they will need to proceed further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if persons -- if military -- if policemen are being sent to the area of Kumanovo, do you think that's because they are needed somewhere in the southern part of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my experience, from when I was working with the Ministry of Interior and even before the year 2000, there have been cases that such type of telegrams are sent, even specifically to the SVR Kocani, where I was working until 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, see, the problem is this telegram is being sent on the 11th of June, 2001, following information received the day before about casualties. Can we agree, Professor Taseva, that in June of 2001 the security situation in Macedonia was very complex. Can we agree on that much?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the security situation in Macedonia at that time was complex, but I really couldn't give any assessment of any relation or link between any documents when I have insufficient elements to make such assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Even though you are a professional -- excuse me, you are a professor of law and you have spent, I think it might be 19 years as an analyst in the Ministry of Internal Affairs, analysing information, you're unable to make the connection between these two documents. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely the fact that, for many years I have been an analyst and I am now a professor who works with elements of events of crimes and definitions thereof, do not give me the right to be involved in any assessment of anything related to this specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender what is 65 ter 965.8, the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is the information of the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P575, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is 65 ter 956.7. And if we could distribute what is the Prosecution's third binder with respect to this witness, then Your Honours will see a hard copy of this document at tab 230.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you could take a look at this document, it will be at tab 30 [sic] in the binder. It's tab 230. And, Professor, do we have another translation problem in the English translation, the same problem that we had before?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The sector is called sector for analytics and research.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ah, okay. And this is a document dated the 12th of June, 2001. It's an information on reports received by the headquarters of operative action Ramno, in connection with the current situation in the Republic of Macedonia between 1500 hours on 11 June and 0700 hours on 12 June 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the second paragraph refers to fighting around the Gjorce Petrov police station. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is there another -- can we scroll down, please, so I can see perhaps the bottom of the English version because I may be missing something. Yes. And it appears this is only one page. Can the court officer confirm that for me, please. This is just a one-page document? No. Okay. And if we could scroll down to the bottom of the second page, please, you'll see, Professor, there's a paragraph starting with: "On 11 June 2001 ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "On 11 June 2001 at 2100 hours, the headquarters of SVR Tetovo rang the headquarters of operative action Ramno and reported that a police patrol was attacked at 2035 hours near the village of Odri by terrorists with automatic weapons while returning to Tetovo from the village of Vratnica." And then it says: "Six reservist and active police officers were injured as a result of the attack. Four of them were transferred to the medical centre in Tetovo with minor injuries while the other two have not been brought as yet and there are no reports regarding their injuries." Have you been following me, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see, then, below that, that this information was dispatched to the minister of the interior, his deputy and a number of other high-ranking members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, I am missing one document which I will find hopefully very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting my colleague Dan Saxon, but on page 43, line 4 of the transcript it was recorded that in the document it was registered that there have been fights in the police station Gjorce Petrov but it cannot be read from the document and I think that my colleague is misleading the witness with regards to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My transcript says around the police station rather than in it. But even that, I think, is not an accurate statement of what is in the paragraph. I think we have all read the paragraph and can see what it is saying. Thank you, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we -- I apologise, Your Honour. Can we pull on the screen Exhibit P468. No, I apologise, this is the wrong document. Can we bring on the screen, please, 65 ter number 966.12. No. Okay, I will move on, Your Honours, and I will come back to this point in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another topic, if we can, Professor Taseva. And just so that I understand your evidence, you discuss in your expert report around paragraph 17 the question of joint operations. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in 2001, you never participated in any joint police or army actions, did you, or operations?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have not participated in any operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And at paragraph 17 of your report, you say the following: "In joint operations of the army and police forces, a joint commander could legally be appointed, whereby members of the police forces would be subordinated to the army." And as authority for that proposition, you cite to a number of pages of transcript of this trial. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This proposition in the first sentence of paragraph 17, it's not expressly stated in any law, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What you say in the first sentence of paragraph 17, that joint operations of the army and police -- that in joint operations of the army and police forces, a joint commander could legally be appointed, whereby members of the police forces would be subordinated to the army, that principle is not expressly stated in any law, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically this is stated in the Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then why don't you cite to the Law on Defence as authority for this proposition?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
