utterances.text: Since that was written below, further below, after paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So are you saying that Article 15 of the Law on Defence -- in Article 15 of the Law on Defence we will find authority for what you say in the first sentence of paragraph 17?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that the Law on Defence has been cited to below and the Law on Defence is also included in the list of references previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where in the Law on Defence - can you tell us please - does it say that in joint operations of the army and police forces, a joint commander could legally be appointed, whereby members of the police forces would be subordinated to the army?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the law in front of me, so I can't give you the answer right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I will move on. You say in the second sentence of paragraph 17: "Nothing" -- and, again, we're talking about joint operations. "Nothing in the constitution or any other law would prevent the president himself to command or direct a joint operation." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as authority for that proposition in footnote 20, you refer to the testimony of General Jovanovski saying: It is not customary practice for the president to be in command of joint operations but the president has the right to decide whether he personally would take command or issue an order to somebody else to command. When you wrote that last sentence in paragraph 17, you were relying, weren't you, on a principle of legal interpretation that basically says if the law does not expressly prohibit the president from doing something, then he can do it. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then, can you explain why you wrote that last sentence then.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the constitution of the Republic of Macedonia expressly states that the president of the state is the supreme commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Right. However, the constitution of Macedonia doesn't expressly state that the president can command or direct a joint operation, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is completely the opposite: That can he command and direct operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I guess I'm more interested in your -- your -- sort of your -- the way you're thinking, the way you were thinking when you wrote this sentence. Because you said, Well, nothing in the constitution or in any other law would prevent the president from doing something. And couldn't we also apply that reasoning to other activities carried out by other Macedonian government officials; for example, if there's nothing in the law that -- or the constitution that would prevent an official from doing activity X, then he or she can do it. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not agree, and this is not the way I understand things. In this case, we have a situation where the constitution expressly states that the president is the supreme commander. And both the report and my statements before this Tribunal yesterday and today state or speak about the positions of other office holders within the government of the Republic of Macedonia and the way in which everything works pursuant to the legislation and the by-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, but maybe you didn't understand my question, because what I said to you was I was really interested in the way you were thinking when you wrote that sentence in paragraph 17. Why was it important for you to note that there's nothing in the constitution or laws that would prevent the president from doing something; in this case, command or direct a joint operation?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was asked to make an analysis of the legal system which covers this topic, having in mind the practice which was presented here earlier by people who testified before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understand that, but, again, you haven't answered my question. I'll ask it one more time. Why was it important to you when you were drafting this sentence to note that there's nothing in the constitution or other laws that would prevent the president from doing something?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt that this is a manner which can express the position of the president, the constitutional and the legal position of the president, in the conditions that were the topic of my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, the same principle should apply to other members of the Macedonian government, shouldn't it? You could apply this manner, this manner of expressing the legal position of the president, also to government ministers, couldn't you? You could say, Well, there's nothing in the constitution or any other law that would prevent Minister Boskoski from carrying out activity X, then he or she can do it. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not agree. Because this report contains an analysis of the legal positioning of the minister in the government of the Republic of Macedonia and the competencies of a minister which are precisely regulated by a number of laws and by-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely. And when you sat down as an expert to write your analysis, you had to make some intellectual decisions, didn't you, as to how you would interpret the constitution and the laws of Macedonia, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume that the writing of any report is an intellectual activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And one can make a decision when writing an expert report to interpret laws narrowly and restrictively, or one can make a decision as to whether to interpret laws more broadly, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisions about how we write about something we wish to explain, I presume are reached on the basis on the expectations of the details we're required to present on that given topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you wrote in paragraph 17 that: "Nothing in the constitution or any other law would prevent the president himself to command or direct a joint operation," you were implementing a broad interpretation of the laws, weren't you? You were saying if it is not expressly prohibited, then it can happen. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I'm asking you to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I did not implement a broad interpretation here but, rather, a strict and specific interpretation of a legal provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, constitutional provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a different topic, if I may. I'd like to talk to you now about the tasks and obligations of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. And in paragraph 28 of your report, you lay out the general obligations of the ministry, and you note the 19 different tasks or obligations that fall within the remit of the Ministry of Interior. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, please, what is Exhibit P00045. This is at tab 34 of the first Prosecution binder, which we can distribute now. If we're missing a binder, I can provide my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Professor Taseva, I don't know if you've ever seen this document before. It's called the White Book: Terrorists of the so-called NLA. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, it's at tab 34 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could go to what is page 9, please. That is the start of the introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see the first page of the introduction and if we could go another page forward, please. I need to see it in the English version. And one more page forward, please. And at the bottom of -- if you go one page back in the Macedonian version, please. And you'll see, Ms. Taseva, that at the end of the introduction, we're told that: "The White Book on the terrorism of the so-called NLA aims to promote the truth regarding the activities of the so-called human rights and democracy fire-fighters of the so-called NLA in the Republic of Macedonia. It aims to tell the true motives and objectives as well as to condemn the atrocities and acts of violence and terror as not appropriate for democracy for civilised societies and for universal human values." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Help us understand, please, where do the laws and regulations of the Ministry of Internal Affairs say that the ministry can or should use government resources to publish "White Books" like this?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who published this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Interior can, within the framework of its activities, to publish analysis, information, publications.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where do we find that in the laws and regulations?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably - I cannot be more specific on this occasion - in the by-laws, which pertain to the unit for analytics and research, of which I spoke earlier. I'm speaking at the top of my head at the moment. This should be studied more in depth to see where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move forward, please, to page 11. And here we see facts about Macedonia; geography, et cetera. Can we move forward to page 15. Professor Taseva, when you said that it is with the by-laws of the Ministry of Internal Affairs provide for the possibility of publishing reports, that would be reports related to the activities of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are reports which pertain generally to the security situation in the Republic of Macedonia, not just the activities of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Here we have a -- we're actually in a chapter now called chronology of historical events. And if we could go back one page, please. No, actually, if we could move to the top of this page. I can't see the top of the page. That's the top? Can we move back one page, please. And one page back in the Macedonian version. Thank you. You'll see there, Professor Taseva, there's a paragraph related to 360/59 B.C.; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I'm not going to read the whole paragraph but it just begins: "Philip the II, the greatest man that Europe has ever given, united Macedonia and enforced Macedonian dominance upon the neighbouring nations." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where do the laws and regulations of the Ministry of Internal Affairs say that the ministry should publish opinions about who was the greatest man in Europe?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it is written that certain services of the ministry or the ministry will provide information, there is no limitation in terms of the time-frame for which this analysis will be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you think this particular time-frame in this analysis will help people understand the security situation in Macedonia in 2001 or 2002?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. We would have to look at the whole context and not take things out of context. Perhaps yes; perhaps no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If that's your evidence I'll move on to another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go to the top -- can we go to page 17, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the top of this page in the English version where we see Roman numeral VII, I think we need to move a bit more in the Macedonian version. Now it's at the bottom of the page in Macedonian. Under Roman numeral VII it says that: "The process of ethnogenesis of the modern Macedonian people, by mixing of the natives and the Slavs, the classical Macedonians started." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do processes of ethnogenesis fall within the remit of the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I will say that I don't understand the overall context. I'm looking at this White Book for the first time. And I cannot comment things seen out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you are testifying here today as an expert on the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Macedonia. You submitted a detailed report. Can you please just tell us whether, can be just yes or no, does the process of ethnogenesis form part of the remit of the Ministry of Internal Affairs? Or if you don't know, you can say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is somehow related to ending the situation from the point of view of preparing strategic analysis, perhaps it can have some relevance but I really cannot say without knowing the content of the whole document and the context in which it has been prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 31, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Here we have a chapter entitled: Facts about national minorities in the Republic of Macedonia. And we have all kinds of census results, percentages, graphs. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where in the laws and the regulations of the ministry does it say that the Ministry of Internal Affairs should publish information about demography? Does it say that anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information about demography are sometimes very important when making decisions related to the policy of crime and strategic orientations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. But there's nothing in the laws or regulations of the Ministry of Internal Affairs that expressly says that the ministry should take care about demography, is there?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all serious security institution, and especially for the Ministry of Interior the question of demographics is extremely important when trying to establish security on the territory of the whole state. Therefore, I believe that this information are indeed important, and as an analyst I can say that not only demographic data but also other data are essential in order to make an adequate security assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where in the Law on Internal Affairs does it say that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a competency of the sector for analytics and research. This is why I corrected you in the translation that this is not investigation, rather, research.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where will we find this competency in regulations or by-laws?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the by-laws of the Ministry of Interior, in the segment pertaining to the sector for analytics and research.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, Professor Taseva, that sometimes the Ministry of Internal Affairs, particularly in that complicated time-period of 2001, undertook activities that are not expressly provided for in the laws and regulations. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This type of information definitely falls within the remit of the ministry, of the work of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, information about who was the greatest man in Europe?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole context of the content is important. Not just one single sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one more time. Sometime in 2001, the Ministry of Internal Affairs undertook activities that were not expressly provided for in the Law on Internal Affairs, or other laws. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the competency of the Ministry of Interior and the services for analytics and research and I don't think that they fall out of the scope of what the law provides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, that's not what I asked you. I want you to answer the question that I asked you. Do you want me to repeat it again?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that these matters are incorporated in the laws and by-laws of the Republic of Macedonia and the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, my understanding is that you're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, I see the time. Shall we take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll resume just after 6.00, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we could briefly could go back to 65 ter Exhibit 956.8, please. This is the report on operative action Ramno from the 10th of June, 2001. If that could be brought up on the screen. And if we could go to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You recall I showed you this report earlier this afternoon, Professor Taseva.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can -- this is dated the 10th of June, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page in the English version, please. And this is 65 ter 956.7? Can we try 65 ter 956.8, please. I think -- yes, this is the report that we saw earlier from the 12th of June, from operative action Ramno. And it's reporting about events on the 11th of June. And if we could turn to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see, again, Professor Taseva, that at the end of this report we see that the police patrol near Tetovo was attacked on the 11th of June. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see that six reserve and active police officers were injured as a result of the attack. And then this -- this information was dispatched to a number of persons at high levels of the ministry, including the minister. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you think this would be an example of reporting information up a chain of command?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is an information produced by the sector of analytics and research within the Ministry of the Interior, and it is the type of information that is produced regularly by the analytics department, and it serves to inform the senior structures in the ministry on the security situation in the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you don't see this as an example of reporting up a -- subordinates reporting up a chain of command to their superiors. You don't -- you don't see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Since here, in this case, the information comes from the sector for analytics within the ministry, and that sector gathers information from all the other sectors in the Republic of Macedonia and from the OVRs. So this is a summary information and not some report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this summary of information was sent up, for example, to the minister, right, and to the directors of the UBK, DBK and the director of public safety bureau, right? Can you just say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I need --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why do you suppose that was? Why do you suppose they sent this information?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since even if you go to the Ministry of the Interior today, will you see that such information, notes are sent to all the aforementioned structures within the ministry on a daily basis because this is the customary procedure to inform about the current security situation within the Republic of Macedonia. So it doesn't have to be the year 2001 or 2008, this is done on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just use your framework just so that we understand. So on a daily basis, information gathered by the ministry, by the analytical sector, is sent to the highest officials of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since those are security-related situations or crime-related situations within the territory of the Republic of Macedonia and this is part of the regular daily information sharing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And help us understand, please, why does the minister and his closest colleagues, why do they need to receive this information on a daily basis? Why is that important?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This type of information that they would receive and that they do receive on a daily basis are important as a basis for decision making, decisions related to the operation of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is Exhibit P00469. Your Honours, it at tab 129, which is in binder 2 from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So we showed you just a moment ago this information related to six police officers who were injured near Tetovo. And here we have a telegram sent on the next day, on the 13th of June, 2001, to the sector of internal affairs, Bitola, sector of finances and other common matters and the sector for analytics and investigation. It's signed by the minister, Ljube Boskoski. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this telegram instructs that 20 policemen and their senior officers be transferred to the premises of the territorial fighting unit in Tetovo by the very next day. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I need to indicate once again that there is a problem about the translation. It is written here territorial fire brigade in the Macedonian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. But can --

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there is a big difference between fighting and fire-fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I haven't read it properly. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's see if we can agree just on this point, though, Professor. That first paragraph says: Sent 20 more policemen and their senior officers up to Tetovo, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what is written, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you think that when the minister sent this telegram on the 13th of June he did it in response to the information that he received on the 12th of June, about the six injured police officers at Tetovo?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that this is the duty of the senior officers in the Ministry of the Interior and of the minister to make the assessment when they need to reinforce certain services if the security situation is at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I take your response, then, as a yes?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if you read these two documents together, wouldn't that be an example of reporting up a chain of command and then issuing an order in response down the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't agree here with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would seek to tender 65 ter 956.8, the report -- the information from the 12th of June, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I assume the counsel meant 65 ter 956.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If that was the prior document that was shown.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit P576.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, I'm grateful for the assistance of the court officer, but the last -- the prior document my case manager informs me was 956.8.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: According to the record, 956.8 is already admitted as Exhibit P575.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that the record becomes clear, can we please call up 956.8. And this is simply a one-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the document of the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you're referring, I believe, to the document of the 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Then I believe the court officer is correct; it would be 956.7. But if we could just see that, just to make sure. If we can go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. Yes. So I would submit then 956.7. I apologise for my error. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit P576?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to a different topic, Professor Taseva. And I'd like to go back to your report for a moment, which is Exhibit 1D309, I believe, and I'd like to focus for a moment on paragraph 45, under the subtitle reservists and volunteers. And the first two sentences of paragraph 45 say this: "In addition to the employees of the ministry, the composition of the police forces may also include reservists. Formally, all reservists of the armed forces, those active in the army and those active in the Ministry of Interior, are engaged by and through the Ministry of Defence." And just so that I understand you, in the beginning of that second sentence, do you use the term "formally" to indicate that you're speaking in the de jure sense?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, during 2001, in practice, didn't the engagement of reservists work a bit less formally?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, see, at that time, during the crisis time in 2001, the Ministry of Internal Affairs had a hard time mobilising sufficient numbers of reserve police officers. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. But this does not mean that when mobilising the procedures do not need to be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But didn't the pressures of those times, Professor, result in individuals deployed as reserve police officers even before all the formal conditions of the laws and regulations for reservists had been fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such cases as well, the procedure was respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you speaking about all cases, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak of all cases, since I'm not aware of specific cases. I'm aware of the overall situation and the position pursuant to the law and regulations on how to act in cases when members of the reserve forces are deployed, and I can only add that these provisions are strictly respected within all activities of this nature in the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about the overall situation in 2001, Professor Taseva. The overall situation was pretty tense and very difficult for the Ministry of Internal Affairs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was tense and difficult for the Ministry of the Interior, but for all people in the Republic of Macedonia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in such difficult circumstances, wouldn't you allow for the possibility that some reservists might have been deployed without the complete fulfilment of all of the conditions laid out in the laws and regulations?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since my experience and my knowledge of this matter speaks that the rules are respected here as expressly stated and very strictly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, in a very stressful time or in an emergency situation, Professor, have you ever bent a rule a little bit?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In a very stressful situation, when you're very tired, in an emergency, have you ever done something that isn't 100 percent in compliance with all the rules?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm asking you to answer, Professor. It's my job to ask questions and it's your job to answer.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I don't find the question sufficiently clear so that I am able to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask it again. In very stressful situations, in situations where you're very tired, you have too much to do, have you ever not completely complied with all of the rules and regulations that relate to the work that you've done?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a definition for this type of conduct in the criminal law. It is also grounds -- grounds for exception. I can't know what the question pertains to. If you're asking me about me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking about you personally.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I really can't answer such abstract question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, just for the record, doesn't appear to be me to be terribly abstract, but I will move on. At paragraph 49 of your report you mention that reservists can be demobilised. And, of course, that would -- that would occur pursuant to the law, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, laws and by-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Right. And then you say this: "Also, it has been the case during the crisis that reservists would return their weapons and equipment and, effectively, be taken out of the reserve. Either way, this would put an end to their relationship with the ministry." You don't cite any authority there. Where is -- where is that practice described in the law?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that is explained in the by-laws pertaining to the deployment of the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why didn't you then cite to the by-laws in your report as authority for this proposition?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in this specific case, the by-law is not cited to. I'm speaking on the basis of my personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you tell us which by-laws refer to this case during the crisis when reservists returned their weapons and equipment and were then taken out of the reserve?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is by-law dealing with such situations in general, not just the situation during crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What does that by-law say?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, see, the problem is, you just told us that -- that there's a by-law that supports what you say here in this paragraph, so it would be very helpful to know where we can find that by-law or what number by-law it is. Can you help us at all with that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Isn't it true, Professor, that in 2001 during the crisis, given the need that you described during your direct examination for efficiency and effectiveness at that difficult time, more informal methods of mobilising and demobilising reservists might have occurred?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would exclude all possibility for informal procedures in these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, in my personal experience, working in the Ministry of Interior, I know how the -- these procedures are positioned and how they function.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You were not working in the Ministry of Internal Affairs during 2001, though, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. I wasn't working there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So during that most difficult time, most complicated time, why do you say you would exclude all possibility for informal procedures in these activities?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because these type of activities are very strictly regulated and based on rules which are very strictly respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: These rules that you haven't cited to in paragraph 49?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to a different topic, if I may. If we can turn, please, to paragraph 54 of your report, Professor Taseva. And this is in the chapter where you discuss the concept of authorised officials. And in paragraph 54, the first sentence says: "It must be made clear that the role and responsibility of 'authorised officials' is further specified in the law and regulations applicable to each category of 'authorised officials,' i.e. the position which he or she holds in the structure." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then in footnote 45 you cite to Articles 1 and 2 of what is Exhibit P0094.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can show that to the witness. This is the guidance for procedure to issue official weapons and special communication equipment to authorised official personnel of the Ministry of Interior. You would find this, Your Honour, in the first Prosecution binder at tab 52, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you see this document, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the title of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if that document is not at the tab that I told you about -- it is? Thank you. And if we could turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see that this guidance was issued on the 7th of April, 1998, for the procedure to issue official weapons and special communication equipment. And, first of all, if we can focus on Article 2, please, towards the bottom of the page. Part 2 is issuing official weapons and then we see Article 2. And it says: "The authorised officials of the police (service), criminal police, directorate for security and counter-intelligence within the ministry and other employees of the ministry who conduct duties and tasks with special responsibilities and authorisations, are personally being issued with official weapons based on a decision brought by the minister of the interior, or after the minister authorises an employee who is managing within the division of finance and other joint matters." Let's stop there for a moment. Can we agree that the first paragraph in Article 2, Professor, it's actually written quite broadly, isn't it, and it indicates that a very large range or category, or different categories, of authorised officials are authorised to receive fire-arms from the ministry, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree. I believe that this provision is very precise because it lists precisely the authorised officials in the police, in the criminal police, in the directorate for security and counter-intelligence, and other employees of the ministry who have authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, in 2001, there were about 9.000 employees of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably your figures are correct. I cannot know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Although I understand that not all employees are authorised officials and I accept that. But the persons, the categories of authorised officials mentioned in that first paragraph, that would include, perhaps, thousands of people, wouldn't it, if not at least hundreds of people, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, all employees in the ministry who are authorised officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now this particular guidance, the beginning of Article 2, it says that: "Authorised officials will be issued an official weapon based on a decision brought by the minister ..." This particular power of the minister to determine who will get an official weapon, that's not expressed in the Law on Internal Affairs, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Ministry of Interior, in this by-law, establishes that authorised officials in the Ministry of Interior are authorised to carry weapons. Therefore, all those who fall under the category of authorised officials are authorised to carry fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I understand that, but it wasn't the question that I asked you. My question was: Nothing in the Law on Internal Affairs expressly says that the minister will make decisions on who will be issued with an official fire-arm. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law states the definition of authorised officials. The by-law, further, regulates who and what are the authorisations and with this one in particular, guidance about the procedure for issuing official weapons, this matter, then, is regulated with the by-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, with all due respect, I think you're evading my question. I'm going to ask it once more. There's nothing in the Law on Internal Affairs that expressly says that the minister will make decisions on who will be issued with an official fire-arm, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law explicitly does not say this. This is regulated with the by-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So not all of the powers and authorisations of the minister of internal affairs are expressly stated in the Law on Internal Affairs, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the legal system of the Republic of Macedonia, the laws do not contain all matters; rather, their implementation is made operational or facilitated through the by-laws. Thus, each concrete law has a large number of associated by-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to Article 6, please, which would be probably the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you -- and could we scroll up to the top of this page, please. We see that there's a subsection 2, and titled cellular phones and pagers. And then we see Article 6. It says this: "The authorised officials of the ministry have the right to use official cellular phones and pagers based on a decision brought by the minister or under-secretary of the minister and the head of the directorate for security and counter-intelligence authorised by the minister." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where does the Law on Internal Affairs, Professor, say that the minister has the right to authorise issuance of cellular phones?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law does not say this explicitly. However, evidently with the development of technology and the needs of the Ministry of Interior, have brought about the need and upgrading in this manual which we're now looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, if the powers of the minister extend to mundane things like issuing cellular phones to employees, to authorised officials, wouldn't it be logical that the minister would also have the power to issue orders on more important matters?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a matter of orders. This is enabling the use of certain equipment. If we go back 12 years in time when this manual was adopted, this equipment was indeed very rare and very expensive. At that time there was probably a need in the ministry to regulate this issue in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Professor, I'll rephrase my question a little bit. If the powers of the minister extend to mundane issues like issuing cellular phones to employees -- to authorised officials, wouldn't it be logical that the minister would also have the power to decide about more important matters.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything which the Law on Internal Affairs and other laws say it's the competency within the ministry and of the minister in particular falls within the realm of issues on which the minister can decide upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. You said a moment ago that matters are not expressly addressed in the Law on Internal Affairs would be covered by the by-laws of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it is not listed in the law that -- where it is stated that by-laws have to be adopted, then these by-laws have to be indeed passed so that the law can be applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the last page of this document, please, so we can see the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see, Professor, this guidance or by-law, if you prefer to call it a by-law, it was signed by the then minister of the interior Tomislav Cokrevski. Help us understand your evidence, please. We have a matter that's not expressly addressed in the Law on Internal Affairs but the minister of the interior can issue by-laws that give him the authority to deal with that matter. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on Internal Affairs states that by-laws will be passed as so the manual for conducting the work in areas pertaining to internal matters that list all authorisations which employees in the Ministry of Interior have and use. One of the authorisations is to use fire-arms. In order for fire-arms to be used, there must be a procedure within which such weapons will be issued to the employees in the ministry, and all of this falls within the frame of the laws, the by-laws, and other acts which regulate this topic, which is legal matter related to the work of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, but I don't think you answered my question. My question was something different. Isn't it true that, if something is not expressly addressed in the laws or the Law on Internal Affairs, the minister himself, and that may be related to powers of the minister or decisions as to what the minister should decide upon, for example, who should receive an official fire-arm. It may be that ministers themselves will issue by-laws or guidances that provide the powers or authorities that they want. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, except that here we have a minister of the interior who's issued a by-law. It's not covered in any laws. So I'm just wondering how this happens, where this authority comes from.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have attempted earlier to explain where this authority comes from. The law contains the term "authorised official," and enumerates the categories of authorised officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The law doesn't say anything about who can receive a fire-arm, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. This is elaborated in the manual for carrying out the work of internal matters. There, all authorisations are explained, authorisations which an authorised official can have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, that manual for carrying out the work of internal matters, that would be approved by the minister, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is adopted by the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to start a different topic. I'm willing to commence it, if you prefer or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suspect that we may proceed more quickly in the long run if we break now, rather than press on for the few remaining minutes. That, though, brings me to the question, Mr. Saxon, of your expected time in cross-examination. Are you able to give an indication?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I was afraid that that question was coming. Your Honour, I believe I need at least two more sessions. I might need more; it's difficult to say right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it that you expect to finish your cross-examination tomorrow or is that merely your hope? This isn't a cross-examination, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understand. It is my hope, Your Honour, to finish tomorrow, and I will do everything that I can to finish tomorrow. I might finish before the end of the day tomorrow. I have to review a lot this evening and early tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In light of Mr. Saxon's indication, Ms. Residovic, you will know whether you need any time in re-examination or not. The Chamber would indicate that if it is the case that the professor has not concluded her evidence tomorrow, that her evidence may be interrupted to allow her to attend to another matter on, we believe, Monday and Tuesday. We give that indication now so that she can make plans and so that you can make plans to have other witnesses available.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if my learned colleague finishes tomorrow within two sessions, so if the third session remains, I will certainly be able to finish the re-direct within that third session. I would prefer if the witness finishes tomorrow. Then, perhaps, Your Honour, proposal would be to have one session in the afternoon, if that is possible. If not, then in my -- in the previous discussions and also in our address to the Chamber, we provided for the possibility that you mentioned also, that the witness could return and we continue on Thursday and we other witnesses for Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Residovic. I'm sure that all of us, especially the -- the professor, would hope that matters may conclude tomorrow, but you will appreciate, as we do, that Mr. Saxon would be very hard pressed, I know he is accepting the burden of trying to achieve it but he would be very hard pressed to conclude his cross-examination in two sessions tomorrow. So we just live in hope that that can be accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. We resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
